Part 1 asks what a claim in social science is for, why people describe the field as being in crisis, and what open research proposes to do about it. It brings in the evidence of the SCORE programme, the five analysts who reanalysed the claim that the day works on, and the archives, repositories and registries in which the data, code and plans of a study are kept. The hands-on work comes at the end and runs into the first break, so that if your machine gives trouble you miss none of the talk. The part takes ninety minutes.

## 1. The plan of the day

**On the slides.** The facilitator sets out the plan of the day and its two kinds of aim, what you will understand and what you will be able to do. The slides also say what you do not need: no installation, no git and no accounts. Open the browser lab in a tab and leave it to load while the facilitator talks.

[Open the browser lab](../../cases/eu-frames/lab.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"}

## 2. The credibility of social science

**On the slides.** Follow the talk on what social science is for, on false positives and forking paths, and on the evidence from replications and many-analysts studies. It goes on to incentives and questionable research practices, and to why the worry is structural rather than a matter of fraud. It then turns to the red-card study, in which twenty-nine teams analysed one dataset, with the estimates that they returned, and ends on why people speak of more than one 'replication' crisis.

## 3. The three Rs and open research

**On the slides.** The word 'replication' names three different operations, which the slides set out as a matrix of data against analysis. The slides then turn to repeatability and credibility, with a quick check on the matrix in peer review, and to the practices of open research, each with the obstacle that it removes.

## 4. SCORE and Multi100

**On the slides.** The SCORE programme ran three studies, of reproducibility, robustness and replicability, and the slides give the results of each and say why the three verdicts do not go together. The slides then present Multi100 from the position of an analyst inside it: what an analyst received, the paper in brief, the two tasks and how the results of the two tasks were put on one scale. A forest plot of the five analysts of the claim follows, with the software and the document format that each analyst used.

## 5. The infrastructure of open research

**On the slides.** The slides cover the archives, statistical offices, repositories and registries in which the materials of research are kept. The slides then set out the data of the case and the terms on which the data are held, which decide what a reproduction can use.

## 6. The SCORE dossier

[Open the SCORE dossier on the OSF](https://osf.io/h7432/){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

When the slides reach the dossier, open it and find the deposit of the analyst whose result you would like to reproduce in Part 3.

## 7. The browser lab and the workspace

**On the slides.** The slides compare the browser lab with the workspace and say what the tools cannot do.

## 8. Task 1 and the warm-up

[Open the browser lab at Task 1](../../cases/eu-frames/lab.qmd#task-1-setup){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

Task 1 is the setup check. Wait for the R engine, run the setup cell, and check that it reports 270 rows, 27 countries and 10 years. The [warm-up](../../cases/eu-frames/lab.qmd#task-1-concepts-warm-up-while-the-engine-loads) gives you something to do while the engine downloads, with four scenarios to label, three of which describe one of the three Rs while the fourth describes something else. If you have installed the workspace, open its folder in your IDE instead and run `source("R/check_setup.R")`. If you need more time, carry on into the break.

**By the end of the part** you can tell apart the three operations that go under the single word 'replication', you know where the materials of a published study are kept and on what terms, and you have R running in the browser lab with the panel of 270 country-years loaded.
